source.filename: 2020_Soft Humanoid Hands with Large Grasping Force Enable by flexible Hybrid Pneumatic Actuators.pdf

constitutive_assumptions: Radial expansion of the inner rubber tube is fully restricted by the constraining rings, maintaining a constant outer diameter and a circular bending arc profile.
Chamber inner diameter increases during elongation and bending while chamber wall thickness changes uniformly under applied air pressure.
Circumference of the inner bladder wall remains smooth and the chamber centerline offsets by eccentricity distance e upon bending.
The bladder wall bonded/contacting the leaf spring undergoes negligible length change, meaning the bending neutral layer coincides with the leaf spring.
Constraining rings act as hinges fixed at contact points along the leaf spring, rotating freely without exerting blocking moments or friction on the bladder.
Rubber bladder material is isotropic and incompressible with a Poisson ratio of 0.4 to 0.5.
Chamber elastomeric deformation is captured by a linear elastic model for tensile strains below 70%.
control_variables: Tensile testing speed (1 mm/min) and room temperature testing conditions
Fatigue testing parameters (bending angle of 180 degrees and cyclic frequency of 1 Hz)
Actuator geometric dimensions held constant when assessing single-factor parameter variations
Thumb installation angle fixed at 75 degrees relative to the hand palm
dependent_variables: Bending deformation profile and bending radius
Blocked actuation force along the actuator length
Normal output force under varying pressures and pre-bending angles
Bladder chamber wall thickness and cross-sectional area
Grasping capability across diverse object masses, shapes, and textures

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: A modular flexible hybrid pneumatic actuator incorporating an inner elastic bladder, rigid outer constraining rings, and a leaf spring backbone achieves high lateral/transverse stiffness while retaining axial bending flexibility.

An analytical mechanics model combining Euler-Bernoulli beam theory, volume conservation, and an empirical swelling correction predicts bending deformation with circular arc fitting errors below 0.86%.
An individual FHPA finger weighing approximately 50 g generates up to 15 N of output force and a 275-degree bending angle at 0.3 MPa air pressure, with an operating frequency exceeding 3 Hz.
Actuation output force scales with chamber count, reaching a maximum force of 42 N at 0.3 MPa for a four-chamber configuration.
Ring geometry directly influences bending mechanics: increasing torus ring thickness enhances bending angle, whereas increasing cylindrical ring thickness reduces bending angle.

Leaf spring material presents a tradeoff between force output and cyclic durability: 65Mn spring steel produces greater output force but suffers brittle fracture after 26,400 cycles, while SUS301 stainless steel survives 41,400 cycles before bladder rupture.
A 350 g five-DOF soft humanoid hand equipped with five FHPAs accomplishes both pinch and enveloping grasps on objects weighing between 3 g and 1366 g.

experimental_setup: Fabrication of FHPAs using 3D-printed ABS constraining rings and end covers, latex or silicone rubber tubing sealed with aluminum alloy plugs, and 65Mn spring steel or SUS301 stainless steel leaf springs.
Pneumatic control system comprising proportional valves (ITV0050-3BS) and solenoid valves (SMC-PSE560) regulating actuation air pressure from 0 to 0.3 MPa.
Deformation and bending angle measurement using six optical markers tracked by an Optotrak 3D motion capture system and a tip-mounted MPU-6050 gyroscope sensor.
Tensile mechanical characterization on a displacement-controlled testing machine at 1 mm/min loading rate up to 75% elongation.
Force characterization using a 100 N force sensor on an adjustable slide for blocked force (L = 0 to 60 mm in 4 mm increments) and a 6D force sensor on a cross slide for normal output force.
Internal and contact deformation observation via Caliper-Quantum FX High Resolution CT scanner with Analyzer image measurement software.
Fatigue durability testing measuring cycle count to failure at 180-degree bending and 1 Hz frequency.
Humanoid hand prototype testing: 350 g, 5 DOFs (four symmetrically distributed fingers and one central thumb tilted at 75 degrees with dual chambers), grasping objects up to 1.366 kg.
future_work: Applying the soft humanoid hand to practical tasks such as fruit picking, product packaging, agricultural harvesting, and fragile object manipulation.
independent_variables: Constraining ring geometry (cylindrical vs. torus profile, ring thickness t, ring gap clearance d)
Actuator body length l (20 to 60 mm)
Actuation force arm height H (9 to 29 mm)
Leaf spring dimensions (thickness h, width b)
Chamber diameters (outer diameter D1, inner diameter D2)
Material selection (latex vs. silicone bladder; 65Mn spring steel vs. SUS301 stainless steel leaf spring)
Number of pneumatic chambers (single, dual, triple, and four chambers)
Force sensor measurement position L along the actuator length
Actuator pre-bending angle during normal force evaluation
limitations_inferred: The analytical model assumes linear elasticity and circular curvature, which does not inherently capture rubber hyperelasticity, localized ring-gap bulging, or contact friction.

The model relies on an empirical adjustment factor (delta S) calibrated against experimental data to correct for chamber bulging between rings, limiting purely predictive modeling for novel ring geometries without initial testing.
Grasping validation was limited to static pick-and-hold demonstrations without closed-loop force, tactile, or slip regulation.
Total system mass and portability exclude off-board compressors, solenoid valves, and proportional pressure regulators.
limitations_stated_by_authors: Completely soft pneumatic actuators exhibit poor resistance to sharp objects, low stability with unbalanced loads, weak output forces for heavy loads, and large required air volumes.
Elastomer hysteresis causes a maximum bending angle deviation of 19.8% between inflation and deflation phases.
Actuator self-weight and contact friction between the bladder and constraining rings cause deflation bending angles to be slightly larger than inflation bending angles.
At pressures above 0.15 MPa, the theoretical model deviates slightly from experimental measurements due to outward rubber bulging in gaps between rings.
65Mn spring steel backbones are brittle and fail prematurely during high-deformation fatigue testing (breaking after 26,400 cycles).
Larger chamber diameters require longer inflation times to reach the desired operating pressure.
Stainless steel backbones undergo slight plastic deformation (approximately 5 degrees off-center) after high-cycle fatigue testing.
main_results: The fabricated FHPA finger (~50 g) attained a maximum bending angle of 275 degrees and an output force of 15 N at 0.3 MPa, operating at frequencies above 3 Hz.
Experimental deformation closely matched circular arc profiles, with circle-fitting errors of 0.86%, 0.69%, and 0.35% at 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 MPa, respectively.
The proposed analytical model closely predicted bending deformation, showing good agreement with experimental data especially at pressures below 0.15 MPa.
Blocked force peaked at an intermediate location along the finger (L ≈ 20 mm) and scaled with applied air pressure.
Torus-shaped constraining rings increased bending angle with increasing ring thickness, whereas cylindrical rings exhibited the opposite trend.
Increasing actuator length increased bending angle (approx. 20 degrees per 10 mm length increase) but decreased output force.
Increasing force arm height H reduced bending angle and yielded negligible force increases beyond H = 15 mm, identifying H = 8 to 14 mm as the optimal range for lengths under 60 mm.
Wider and thicker leaf springs decreased bending deformation while increasing normal output force.

Silicone bladders generated larger bending deformation than latex bladders due to lower modulus, while 65Mn spring steel produced higher forces than stainless steel at the expense of fatigue resistance.
Four-chamber FHPA configurations achieved normal output forces up to 42 N at 0.3 MPa.
The assembled 350 g, 5-DOF soft humanoid hand demonstrated secure pinch and enveloping grasps across items weighing from 3 g (table tennis ball) up to 1366 g (bottled juice).
modeling_methods: Euler-Bernoulli beam bending theory for resisting moments of the leaf spring and elastomeric bladder
Linear elastic mechanical model for the bladder under strains below 70% based on tensile stress-strain characterization
Static moment equilibrium formulation equating pneumatic actuation moment to the sum of leaf spring and rubber tube resisting moments
Material incompressibility and volume conservation formulation incorporating an empirical cross-sectional area correction factor (delta S) for gap bulging
Circular arc curvature kinematics relating actuator bending radius to original length and bending angle
performance_metrics: Radius fitting error percentage relative to a circular arc (%)
Hysteresis deviation percentage between inflation and deflation (%)
Blocked actuation force and normal output force (N)
Total hand mass and individual finger mass (g)
Maximum grasping payload capacity (g or kg)
Fatigue cycle count to failure under cyclic bending
possible_gap_implications: The need for an empirical correction factor to account for inter-ring bulging highlights an opportunity for non-linear finite element or analytical hyperelastic contact models that inherently predict localized bulging.
The absence of integrated sensory feedback suggests an opportunity to integrate flexible strain, curvature, or tactile sensors for closed-loop grasping control.

Fatigue failure in spring steel and bladder rupturing under cyclic loading indicate that exploring fatigue-resistant composite backbones and durable elastomeric compounds remains an open engineering challenge for long-term industrial deployment.
paper.research_objective: To design, model, fabricate, and experimentally evaluate a modular flexible hybrid pneumatic actuator (FHPA) and assemble a five-DOF soft humanoid hand capable of robustly grasping items of diverse weights, sizes, shapes, textures, and stiffnesses with high grasping force, rapid response, low cost, and ease of assembly and maintenance.
paper.research_problem: Traditional rigid robot grippers can damage delicate objects and present collision hazards during human-robot interaction, while conventional purely soft pneumatic grippers suffer from low grasping force, poor stability when holding unbalanced loads, vulnerability to sharp objects, and large air volume requirements. Furthermore, prior hybrid designs often exhibit slow actuation speeds, complex mold-casting manufacturing, or limited fatigue durability.
stiffness_mechanism: leaf spring elastic backbone (transverse stiffness with axial flexibility)
outer rigid constraining rings (radial expansion constraint)
paper.title: Soft Humanoid Hands with Large Grasping Force Enabled by Flexible Hybrid Pneumatic Actuators
